query: For high-entropy alloys intended as intermediate materials in plasma-facing reactor components, what single intervention could improve heat-transfer capability while preserving structural integrity? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the expected outcome compared with current intermediate-layer performance, the temperature and loading conditions under which it should hold, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled high-temperature forging and annealing treatment applied to tungsten-based high-entropy alloy intermediate layers will enhance heat-transfer capability by reducing grain boundary scattering while retaining structural integrity through a tuned nanoprecipitate network.
generation.material_initial_state: Tungsten-based high-entropy alloy produced via conventional processing (e.g., additive manufacturing with rapid solidification) used as an intermediate layer in plasma-facing reactor components.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled thermomechanical treatment consisting of forging at 900–1200 °C with intermediate cool-down intervals followed by a tailored annealing step to promote partial recrystallization and optimized nanoprecipitate distribution.
generation.conditions: High-temperature plasma-facing reactor environment with elevated temperatures (≥ 900 °C) and high mechanical loads, simulating operational reactor conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: A partially recrystallized matrix featuring a refined, coherent nanoprecipitate network that minimizes excessive grain boundary density.
generation.mechanism: The high-temperature forging reduces defect density and refines the microstructure, while controlled annealing promotes nanoprecipitate formation that reduces heat carrier scattering. This combination is hypothesized to improve thermal conductivity without compromising the alloy’s strength and ductile performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to standard processing, the treated alloy is expected to exhibit improved thermal conductivity (from reduced boundary scattering) and a comparable yield strength and ductility, ensuring its suitability as an intermediate layer under reactor conditions.
generation.baseline: Intermediate layers processed by conventional additive manufacturing and heat treatments that prioritize mechanical stability but do not target enhanced thermal transport.
generation.boundary: The benefits are predicted to hold under high-temperature (900–1200 °C) and high mechanical load conditions typical of plasma-facing reactor environments; deviations in processing parameters outside the specified regime may not yield the desired thermal or structural performance.
generation.uncertainty: It is currently uncertain how sensitive the balance between improved heat transfer and mechanical integrity is to slight variations in forging and annealing parameters; additional optimization may be required to precisely control the nanoprecipitate network.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of tungsten-based high-entropy alloy samples: one set processed using conventional methods and a second set subjected to the targeted high-temperature forging (900–1200 °C with intermediate cooling) followed by the controlled annealing treatment. Expose both sets to high-temperature (≥ 900 °C) and high mechanical load testing conditions simulating the plasma-facing environment.
measurements: Thermal conductivity using laser flash or comparable thermal diffusivity measurements
Yield strength and ductility via high-temperature tensile tests
Microstructural analyses (optical/SEM imaging) to quantify grain size, recrystallization, and nanoprecipitate distribution
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermomechanically treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in thermal conductivity over the conventional samples without a corresponding decrease in yield strength and ductility under the defined test conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

However, the rapid solidification process also leads to increased internal stress and reduced structural stability in the components. Therefore, this study focuses on the AlFeCoCrNi2.1 EHEA as the research subject, utilizing laser additive manufacturing to fabricate components and systematically investigating the influence of heat treatment processes on the microstructure and mechanical properties of the components. The research demonstrates that low-temperature heat treatment (700 °C and below) acts as a stress relief-annealing process for the components. The yield strength decreased from 1003.2 MPa to 742.1 MPa. At 900 °C heat treatment, the constraining effect between recrystallized grains and surrounding grains outweighs the dislocation release effect caused by recrystallization, resulting in an increase in dislocation density. decision.trend: Recent tungsten-based high-entropy alloy studies focus on improving mechanical performance under extreme temperatures and stresses by controlling microstructure, either via powder metallurgy or through stepwise coherent nanoprecipitations. While these methods have successfully enhanced strength and ductility for plasma-facing applications, they have not explicitly optimized heat-transfer capabilities. Achieving higher thermal conductivity while retaining mechanical robustness remains a focal challenge.
decision.unsolved: Simultaneously boosting thermal transport and preserving structural integrity in tungsten-based high-entropy alloys for plasma-facing components has not been thoroughly addressed, leaving open questions about how to engineer microstructural features that both improve conductivity and maintain mechanical durability in reactor environments.
decision.lever: Adopt a controlled high-temperature forging and subsequent annealing sequence to promote partial recrystallization and refine second-phase distributions. For example, forging at 900–1200 °C with intermediate cool-down intervals can yield a partially recrystallized matrix and a tuned nanoprecipitate network. This reduces boundary scattering of heat carriers while retaining strength through stable precipitates and balanced grain-boundary configurations.
decision.why: Building on work that improved mechanical integrity via microstructural tailoring, a targeted thermomechanical approach can reduce defect density and refine precipitates, mitigating thermal scattering without compromising mechanical performance. This strategy directly addresses the gap in current literature by enhancing heat-transfer properties while preserving the alloy’s structural integrity under high-temperature, high-stress plasma-facing conditions.
